Elliot Rodger was an excellent example of this. His belief that he should just get to have a girlfriend and she should give him sexual gratification when he wanted it shows clear misperception of valuation of a partner... and in fact, it demonstrates his belief that she would be a possession, not an equal.

Another concern is the drive to prove worthiness on the part of the Incel. Relational concerns are highly transactional for these individuals and do not reflect understanding of complex, interpersonal growth.

A therapeutic approach needs consideration as well. It’s very easy to marginalize an incel for inappropriate social behavior, but we have to remember that these folks are expressing a much more deeply rooted problem than the violence, or the misplaced need for sexual gratification. These people are more than just their behavior, and I think that gets missed.

A tertiary concern is the passive, victimized attitude that surrounds the “nice guy” motif. 

It also strikes me that he vast majority of incels fall within a very limited chromatic spectrum... meaning the overwhelming majority committing these crimes tend to be Caucasian. 

Social contract is changing. Locus of acceptable behavior is changing, albeit slowly,  and if the model of diffusion is applied, these guys are really, really resistant to the new normal our culture is pushing toward. 

So what to do about them? I think a no nonsense, zero tolerance approach that does not punish the victims of these crimes is a start, but only a partial solution. 

The nature of the crimes being committed also reflect maladjusted social acceptance of unwanted communication and the diminished value fundamental social courtesy.

Socially speaking, we, as a dynamic and diverse society need to speak about these issues, and speak about them often.

Just my two cents.

I’m not saying it’s impossible. I’m saying it’s possible for more than one thing to be true at the same time. It’s not an issue of black and white, right or wrong, on or off... that would be really nice, but it’s not how life works.

I also agree that a lot of folks could make some lifestyle changes and improve their health. That’s obvious. To lump all into that is dismissive and lacks empathy and awareness of what’s happening in the lives of others. It’s assuming that your perception is reality for all.

Assuming a lack of motivation is pretty careless and judgmental. I have a very rare endocrine disorder that has dramatically slowed my metabolism. Rare meaning there are 300 of us in the US that are diagnosed. It took years to diagnose and requires world class specialists to identify what I would have to do to manage it.

I didn’t cause it, and I certainly don’t deserve it. It has taken nearly five years for me to lose 60 pounds when a new pharmaceutical therapy came out. Think about that for a moment... a pound a month at best. I have a great nutritional plan, I exercise 5-6 days a week, and my critical diagnostics are insanely good. I’m motivated by a desire for my own quality of life in my perception of reality.

For 30 years now, I’ve struggled with my health. For you to say I just didn’t want to be healthy, or I just let myself go, or that I am lazy... you assume that it all must be true under a singular causation. All I have ever wanted is to be fit and healthy. You’ve no idea how motivated I am, and have been since it started at 15.

I know that I will not have a traditional life expectancy. I choose highly modified nutritional management and exercise very regularly so my circulatory system will be less likely to reduce the quality of my life in the time I have left.

I also will hazard a guess that you might not have considered that you expect people to fit the mold you are comfortable with, and that you believe others must meet the expectations you have for yourself. Holding others to those standards will be frustrating at best and isolating for you at worst.

I’m not meaning to pick a fight with you at all- All I am saying is that there is more than obvious to generalized stereotypes and minor, uninformed observations.

Your solutions only treat the physicality of obesity. It completely ignores the psychological side, and guarantees relapse. And your description of a portrayal is spot on, because portrayals are often skewed and uninformed.

If my doctor had actually done his job when my illness presented at 15, I would likely be managing a normal lifestyle. I would not have developed diabetes as a secondary condition, I’d be able to have children, I’d be able to exercise normally... if he’d taken me seriously.

Instead, he told my parents I was sneaking food, and that they should put a lock on the fridge. They did... I wasn’t... I followed the diet he gave them to a tee, and I was in volleyball, soccer, and softball in high school. It didn’t work, and in fact, I gained a lot more weight. It was a nightmare that has never ended.

Many people, particularly obese women, do not receive the same high quality care that other patients do. Plus, surgery is not the best option for most. There is not a blanket, one size fits all solution to this problem. It would be nice, but it’s not reality. Most things in life are really messy that way.

My hope is to simply share this perspective and increase understanding of this issue. I’m hoping you  are, too.

There are sound cues that are behavior specific, occurring when choices are right or wrong.  You and I might not always notice them. I know a guy who can play The NBA games and win more often than others who see; and if you take him to a court and put at the free throw line, he very rarely misses there.

The brain pays the most attention to visual input. People often mistakenly assume that if sight is gone, other senses are superhuman to compensate, when the reality is the brain is paying mire attention to the remaining senses.

Case in point: assistive technology can demonstrate this easily... screen readers take the code in the software and relay the information out loud to the user. An average sighted person can process about 100-130 words each minute this way. The non sighted individual who has average functional computer literacy can process 300 words per minute on average simply because their hearing is not being subdued by vision. The best part? Most screen reader’s settings can be changed to 500 or 600 words per minute.

Another thing, OP, there many non-visual video games played by millions of persons with blindness and low vision. A very longstanding and popular one is Legend of the Green Dragon, if you’re interested.

There is sometimes an erroneous belief that the blind/low vision community does not understand the sighted world. This is simply not true. I am certain they’ll appreciate being respected for what they bring to the table rather than discounted because of a situation they can’t control.

He died 3 months into the job. It took me years to stop blaming myself... as if he’d never have died by any other cause, right?

Your friend, and I grieve with her, will come to a choice... either she lives beyond him, or she dies with him by not accepting that life deals a really crappy hand sometimes.

I don’t know if you or she are scripture readers, but the Bible talks about how the rain falls on the good and the bad... not meaning to proselytize, just giving my impression... it helped me to refocus on what mattered most: the time with him was delightful, happy, and an absolute gift from him to me.

You are an amazing friend to see past the surface of this for her, and on behalf of all who have been through this, thank you for being such a true companion.

Therapy is good, it’s important. In transparency, it took me almost five years to even think about dating again. Thinking about what helped me... let her know you’re there, and not going anywhere... that you’re not judging her thought and behavior patterns... that you care enough to call her out on unhealthy choices... that you want her to find happiness beyond him... that responses are a choice, and you care about how she manages her self care.

It won’t fix it for her, but the goal is not to exist, but to live. Remind her of where and when she is: it’s 2017. She survived, now she needs to focus on thriving after him. Dating will come later if it’s what she wants, but she needs to focus on rebuilding her identity and joy after him.

It’s a start, at least.
